exam: A 30‑year‑old farmer from rural Tanzania presents with a first generalized seizure; what are the three most important bedside questions and why? — Exposure to pork, travel history, and prior seizures; they establish epidemiologic risk, differentiate NCC from other causes, and guide imaging urgency.
CT shows a single ring‑enhancing lesion with surrounding edema; how does this influence your management? — Indicates colloidal stage; start steroids before albendazole and control seizures.
Why is albendazole preferred over praziquantel as monotherapy in NCC? — Better cyst penetration, fewer drug‑interaction issues, and proven efficacy in single‑agent regimens.
A patient with known NCC develops worsening headache and vomiting; what is your next step? — Assess for raised intracranial pressure; obtain urgent imaging and consider neurosurgical referral.
How would you manage NCC in a hospital without MRI or serology? — Rely on clinical epidemiology, CT if available, start empirical albendazole with steroids, and treat seizures.
What are the contraindications to using carbamazepine in NCC patients? — Hepatic impairment, concomitant antiretroviral therapy causing enzyme induction, and risk of severe rash.

Explain the significance of a calcified lesion on CT in a patient with recurrent seizures. — Represents dead cyst; no antiparasitic needed, focus of epilepsy requiring long‑term antiepileptic therapy.
In a co‑infected HIV patient, why might NCC present atypically? — Immunosuppression blunts inflammatory response, leading to fewer symptoms despite viable cysts.
ai.title: Neurocysticercosis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Neurocysticercosis is a parasitic infection of the CNS caused by Taenia solium larvae. It presents with seizures, headaches, and focal deficits, especially in low‑resource tropical settings.

b: Four cyst stages: vesicular, colloidal, granular‑nodular, calcified
Common in East Africa, Latin America, and parts of Asia
Most frequent cause of adult‑onset seizures in endemic areas
sections.p: Ingested eggs of Taenia solium hatch in the intestine, release oncospheres that migrate hematogenously to the brain and form cysts. The disease course depends on cyst stage and host response.

b: Seizure is the presenting symptom in >70% of cases
Colloidal stage cysts cause the most inflammation
Calcified lesions may act as epileptogenic foci
sections.p: Diagnosis hinges on clinical presentation, epidemiology, and neuroimaging. Serology and CSF aid when imaging is unavailable. Treatment combines antiparasitics, steroids, and seizure control.

b: Consider NCC in any patient with seizures from a pork‑eating region
Rule out raised intracranial pressure before starting antiparasitics
Co‑infection with HIV may blunt inflammatory response, altering presentation
sections.p: Patients often present to district hospitals with new‑onset seizures or focal neurologic signs. Recognising NCC guides appropriate use of limited resources and avoids unnecessary antibiotics or surgery.
If CT/MRI are unavailable, rely on clinical epidemiology, seizure pattern, and positive serology. Treat empirically if suspicion is high and other causes are excluded.

t.b: Detects calcified cysts, edema, hydrocephalus; answers whether there is a space‑occupying lesion
Better delineates cyst stage and scolex; answers cyst viability and inflammation
Supports diagnosis when imaging is equivocal; a positive result suggests exposure
Helps exclude meningitis; may show mild lymphocytosis and elevated protein
Elevated eosinophils can hint at parasitic infection when other causes are unlikely

b: Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) started 1–2 days before antiparasitics to blunt inflammation
Phenobarbital or levetiracetam for seizure control; avoid carbamazepine if hepatic disease present
Surgical removal only for large intraventricular cysts causing obstructive hydrocephalus
If imaging unavailable, give albendazole with steroids in patients with seizures and compatible exposure
sections.p: Treat active cysts, control inflammation, and prevent seizures. Adjust therapy to cyst stage and availability of drugs.

b: Stage‑specific imaging: scolex visible → vesicular; ring‑enhancing lesion with edema → colloidal
Steroids are mandatory when treating viable cysts to prevent worsening edema
Calcified lesions are not treated with antiparasitics; manage as epilepsy
sections.p: Focus on epidemiology, cyst stages, imaging findings, and treatment hierarchy. Remember contraindications and drug interactions in low‑resource settings.

b: Assuming all seizures in endemic areas are NCC; rule out meningitis, TB, malaria
Starting antiparasitics without confirming no obstructive hydrocephalus
Neglecting to give seizure prophylaxis after cyst resolution
sections.p: Pitfalls include misreading calcifications as acute lesions, omitting steroids, and using carbamazepine in hepatic impairment.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness, new focal deficit, or signs of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting, papilledema, altered mental status)
